title: Why making things too easy destroys their perceived value: The Alchemy of Meaningful Friction in design and AI.
thesis: When we optimize purely for frictionless speed, we inadvertently destroy perceived psychological value and human connection.

linkedin.content:
Every tech company is racing to eliminate friction.

They're making a massive behavioral mistake.

In the 1950s, Betty Crocker launched instant cake mix. It was a technological marvel: just add tap water, stir, and bake.

It flopped completely.

Why? Because it was too frictionless. When mothers served it to their families, they felt guilty. They felt like frauds.

Then the psychologist Ernest Dichter advised them: Remove the powdered eggs. Make the baker crack a fresh egg into the bowl.

Sales exploded.

Why did adding more work make the product 10x more successful?

Because of three behavioral realities:
1. The IKEA Effect: We place irrational value on things we helped build.
2. Costly Signaling: Unforgeable effort is the only true proof of value.
3. Psychological Ownership: When an outcome requires zero human investment, it leaves zero emotional residue.

If you're building software, content, or AI workflows today:
Stop asking "How can we make this 100% effortless?"
Start asking "Where can we place the meaningful friction that makes people feel proud of their contribution?"

Speed creates commodities. Meaningful friction creates cults.

What's an area where you prefer friction over automation? Let me know below.

twitter_x_thread.content:
Why making things 'too easy' secretly destroys their value 🧵

Every product team is obsessed with frictionless speed.

Here is why that intuition is psychologically backwards (and how behavioral alchemy solves it): [1/5]

In the 1950s, instant cake mixes only required water.

They flopped.

Mothers felt like frauds serving zero-effort food.

When the formula was changed to require cracking a fresh egg, sales skyrocketed.

The egg added physical work—but created psychological ownership. [2/5]

As Rory Sutherland notes: logic says 'less effort = happier human.'

Psychology says: 'zero effort = zero perceived value.'

Biologists call this Costly Signaling Theory. If a signal costs nothing to produce, it carries zero social or emotional weight. [3/5]

When AI generates 100% of an essay or app with 1 click, nobody falls in love with it.

The winning formula isn't passive automation.

It's AI leverage + unforgeable human friction (your conviction, taste, and critique). [4/5]

Stop asking: 'How do we eliminate all friction?'

Start asking: 'Where is the one point of curated friction that gives our users genuine pride of authorship?'
